title: Sati Pali Ontology
description: This ontology follows the public-domain early Buddhist lists preserved in the Pāli Tipiṭaka: the three marks, the four noble truths (SN 56.11), the noble eightfold path (SN 45.8), dependent origination (SN 12.2), the aggregates (SN 22), the sense bases (SN 35), satipaṭṭhāna (MN 10, DN 22), and the thirty-seven bodhipakkhiyā dhammā. The four paramattha dhammas are the later Theravada Abhidhamma division of that same field. The English glosses were written for Sati-AI. They are not copied from a copyrighted dictionary.
creator: Marlon Barrios Solano

terms.definition: The three characteristics of conditioned experience: impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, and not-self. Seeing them clearly is the heart of insight.
Whatever arises changes and ceases. Nothing conditioned stays fixed.
The strain of experience that cannot finally satisfy: pain, change, and the burden of conditioned life. It is the first noble truth, not a claim that every moment feels miserable.
No experience, body, or mind contains a permanent owner. What is seen as 'me' or 'mine' is a changing process.
The framework of the teaching: unsatisfactoriness, its origin, its cessation, and the path to cessation. Each truth has a task: understand, abandon, realize, develop.
The second truth. Craving produces the repeating stress of conditioned life.
The third truth. Unsatisfactoriness ends when craving ends. That end is nibbāna.
The fourth truth: the way of practice that leads to cessation, spelled out as the noble eightfold path.
Thirst for sense pleasure, for becoming, or for getting rid of what is painful. It is named as the origin in the second truth.
Thirst for pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and ideas. One of the three kinds of taṇhā.
Thirst to continue, to be a particular kind of being, or to arrive at a particular state.
Thirst to be rid of what is painful, or for a painful state to stop. It is still craving.
Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and collectedness. Together they are the path truth.
Seeing experience in the light of the four truths, kamma, and not-self, rather than through a fixed identity.
Intention of letting go, of goodwill, and of non-harming.
Speech that abstains from lying, harshness, division, and idle chatter.
Bodily conduct that abstains from killing, taking what is not given, and sexual harm.
Supporting one's life in a way that does not require harm.
Energy that prevents and abandons unwholesome states and arouses and maintains wholesome ones.
Remembering to attend, clearly, to body, feeling, mind, and patterns of experience.
A mind gathered, steady, and bright enough for insight. Classically described through the four jhānas.
Deep states of unified attention. They steady the mind; they are not themselves the goal.
The path gathered into ethics, collectedness, and wisdom. Each supports the others.
Care in speech, action, and livelihood so that the mind is less tangled by harm.
The mind gathered around a wholesome object, neither scattered nor forced.
Direct understanding of impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, and not-self, not only an idea about them.
Nothing arises alone. From not-knowing through feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming, birth and aging-and-death keep turning. When a link is no longer fed, the pattern can cease.
Not seeing the four truths. It is the first link of dependent origination and the last of the ten fetters.
Constructing activities: intentions that shape experience, and, as an aggregate, the mental activities other than feeling and perception.
Knowing through a sense door: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or thinking. It arises with an object; it is not a lasting self.
Mentality and materiality together: the felt, named side of experience and the bodily side, dependent on each other.
Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, meeting their objects: sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental phenomena.
The meeting of a sense base, its object, and the knowing of that meeting. Feeling is born from contact.
The pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful tone of experience. It is not the story about the feeling.
Holding on: to sense pleasure, to views, to rites and habits as if they were the path, and to a doctrine of self.
The momentum of a life taking shape from clinging: a way of being that is already leaning toward the next birth of that pattern.
The appearing of a new identity in a world of experience, whether read as rebirth or as the birth of a self-story.
The ending built into whatever is born: aging, falling apart, grief, and death.
A person, looked at without a hidden owner: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
The bodily, material side of experience, including the body as sensed. As an aggregate it is not the self.
Recognizing and labeling: the mind marking an experience as this or that.
The eye base. With a sight and eye-consciousness, visual contact occurs.
The ear base, the door of hearing.
The nose base, the door of smell.
The tongue base, the door of taste.
The body as the door of touch, and also the whole lived body contemplated in mindfulness of the body.
The mind base. Its objects are dhammas: ideas, memories, images, and mental qualities.
Four fields for remembering to look: body, feeling tone, mind, and patterns of experience.
Remembering. In practice, remembering to be present with what is actually happening, and remembering the teaching while you do.
Knowing what one is doing while doing it: purpose, suitability, and the field of experience one is in.
Using the breath as the anchor for mindfulness, and through it for the body, feeling, mind, and wisdom.
Attending to the body as body: breath, postures, activities, parts, and elements, without turning it into a self.
The four ways the body is disposed: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Mindfulness knows which one is happening.
Looking at the body as a collection of parts, as the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta lists them, so that it is harder to take the body as a polished self.
In mindfulness of the body, earth, water, fire, and air: solidity, cohesion, warmth, and motion, known as qualities rather than as mine.
Remembering a corpse in its stages of decay, and seeing that this body has the same nature. It is a contemplation of impermanence, not a fascination with death.
Knowing a feeling as pleasant, painful, or neutral, worldly or unworldly, as it is.
Knowing the mind's current color: with or without greed, hatred, or delusion; contracted or spacious; concentrated or not.
Watching the categories of experience themselves: hindrances, aggregates, sense bases, factors of awakening, and the truths.
The classical map of the path: four foundations of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of success, five faculties, five powers, seven awakening factors, and the eightfold path.
Effort to prevent and abandon the unwholesome, and to arouse and maintain the wholesome.
Desire to act, energy, mind, and investigation, each joined with effort, so that practice actually develops.
Wholesome interest in doing what is needed. It is not the same as sensual craving.
Looking into how a state actually works, rather than taking it on habit.
Faith, energy, mindfulness, collectedness, and wisdom as governing faculties. As powers, the same five are unshakable.
Trust that leans toward practice, born of understanding rather than blind belief.
Mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, collectedness, and equipoise. Mindfulness starts the set and keeps it balanced.
The awakening factor that looks into mental and bodily events and sorts what leads toward freedom.
Sustained effort that is neither collapse nor strain.
Interested, buoyant joy that refreshes practice. It is stronger and more energetic than quiet happiness.
The pleasant ease that can follow joy when effort softens. It is a feeling tone, and still impermanent.
Calm of body and mind. A factor of awakening, and the quiet that lets collectedness deepen.
Sensual desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt. They cover the mind so that it cannot see clearly.
The hindrance of wanting to pull a pleasant sense experience closer.
The hindrance of pushing away: irritation, hostility, and the wish that something be harmed or gone.
Heaviness of mind and body that sinks attention.
A stirred mind, plus regret that keeps rehearsing what was done or left undone.
Remorse about what was done or left undone. Together with restlessness it is one of the five hindrances.
Paralyzing uncertainty about the practice, not healthy questioning. It is both a hindrance and an early fetter.
What binds a person to the round: identity view, doubt, attachment to rites, sensual lust, aversion, lust for form and the formless, conceit, restlessness, and not-knowing.
Taking one of the aggregates, or the set of them, to be a self.
Clinging to a rule or ritual as if performing it were itself awakening.
The fetter of desire for sensual pleasure. It thins at the once-return and falls away at non-return.
The fetter of resistance and ill will. It is abandoned with the stage of non-return.
The comparison 'I am better, worse, or equal.' It can remain subtly even after gross identity view has fallen.
The subtle stir of the mind. As a fetter it is only fully dropped at arahantship.
Outflows that intoxicate the mind: sensuality, becoming, views, and not-knowing. An arahant is one in whom they have ended.
The outflow of intoxication with sensual pleasure.
The outflow of wanting to continue as a particular kind of being.
The outflow of clinging to a view as if the view were the one who sees.
The root that pulls toward. With hatred and delusion it is one of the three unwholesome roots. Dispassion is its fading.
The fading of passion. In the discourses it stands between clear seeing and the full end of craving.
The Abhidhamma name for the same pulling root more often called rāga in the suttas.
The root that strikes out or pushes away.
The root of not seeing. It is the cloudy side of avijjā.
Four boundless attitudes: goodwill, compassion, joy in others' good, and equanimity.
The wish that beings be well, without needing them to be yours.
The tremble of the heart that wants suffering to ease, in oneself and in others.
Gladness when another being is happy or free. It is the antidote to envy.
Balance that does not lean into grabbing or pushing away. It is the fourth divine abiding, and also an awakening factor.
A person who has seen the truths directly and dropped identity view, doubt, and attachment to rites.
A person in whom sensual lust and aversion have been weakened.
A person who has abandoned sensual lust and aversion.
A person in whom the taints and the remaining fetters have ended. Nothing further is to be done for their own freedom.
The end of greed, hatred, and delusion, and so the end of the fire of dukkha. It is not a place and not a self.
Release. The mind is freed from what bound it, for a time through collectedness or for good through the end of the taints.
A mind released, often through collectedness, from hindrance or from defilement. The discourses pair it with liberation by wisdom.
Release that comes from seeing. It is the understanding side of freedom, named beside liberation of the mind.
Eight ways the mind is released from being stuck on form and on feeling, ending with the cessation of perception and feeling.
The Theravada Abhidhamma division of what is finally real for analysis: consciousness, mental factors, form, and nibbāna. This is a later map laid over the sutta teachings.
The knowing moment itself. In mindfulness of mind, one knows its quality without owning it.
Qualities that arise with a moment of knowing, such as contact, feeling, perception, intention, and the roots.
Intentional action of body, speech, or mind, and the way that intention shapes what follows.
The ripening of intentional action as experience. Result is to be understood, not hated or owned.
The round of birth, aging, and death kept spinning by not-knowing and craving.
Knowing a thing in the way it is, rather than in the way wanting or fear paints it.
Seeing that has become understanding. In the discourses it names a direct knowing, not a borrowed opinion.

terms.gloss: knowledge and vision according to reality
terms.definition: Knowledge and vision of things as they actually are. Insight is aimed at this seeing.
aliases: knowledge and vision of things as they are

terms.definition: Clear seeing of the three marks in present experience. It is a quality of attention, not a brand of technique.
The cultivation of a peaceful, gathered mind. It supports insight and is not a rival to it.
Developing wholesome qualities by bringing them to mind again and again. Meditation is one form of it.
Attending to the root of an experience: what feeds it, and what leads toward freedom rather than toward more clinging.
Care that does not throw life away. The canon treats it as the one condition for all wholesome states.
Giving. It loosens holding and is the natural companion of a teaching offered freely.
In the early texts, emptiness of a self in experience. Later traditions unfold this word much further; here it stays tied to anattā.
Going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha: the teacher, the teaching, and the community of those who have practiced it deeply.
One who has woken up to the way things are, and the historical teacher Gotama whose teaching this ontology records.
Two related uses: the teaching that leads to freedom, and any phenomenon that can be known. The mind's objects are dhammas in the second sense.
The community of practitioners, and in the refuge formula especially those who have entered the noble path.
Waking up. The factors that assist it are the bodhipakkhiyā dhammā.
